beginner: Shallots and carrots are a classic garden pair. The strong allium smell is said to help hide carrots from the carrot rust fly, and the two plants do not crowd each other's roots.

beginner: Beets and shallots grow well side by side. They like the same cool weather and stay out of each other's way.
seasoned: Beets and shallots share a bed comfortably. The allium pungency helps deter pests that bother beets, and because shallots bulb shallowly with sparse upright foliage while beets put their energy into a single root, the two do not crowd each other above or below ground. beginner: Fast little lettuce plants fit nicely in the gaps between shallots and like the same cool season, so you get two crops from one spot.

beginner: Cabbage and broccoli like the same cool weather as shallots, and the strong allium smell is thought to bother some of their pests.

Alliums are shallow and undemanding, so they tuck between brassicas without competing for the heavy feeding those crops want.

This is the stage that decides clump size: the leaf canopy built now sets how many bulbs the clump can make and how large they get. You want vigorous, uninterrupted leaf growth, not a check from drought, weeds, or cold.

beginner: Help the plants grow lots of healthy leaves now. Feed with nitrogen, keep the soil evenly moist, and keep weeds out. Do most of the feeding early, because feeding too late leads to soft necks that do not store well.
seasoned: Push leaf growth: side-dress nitrogen, hold moisture steady, and stay ruthless about weeds. Front-load the feeding so the canopy is built before day length triggers bulbing; nitrogen applied late goes to soft necks instead of bulbs.

beginner: Note when you fed the plants and how many shoots each one makes. More shoots now means a fuller clump later.
seasoned: Track feeding dates and how many shoots each clump throws; that previews how full the clump will be.

beginner: When the days reach the right length, the plant stops making new leaves and each shoot swells into its own bulb, turning one planted set into a clump of several. This switch is set by how long the days are where you live, not by the calendar, so you cannot speed it up.
seasoned: Once day length crosses the cultivar threshold, the plant stops adding leaves and each growing point swells into its own bulb, so a single set becomes a cluster of 6 to 12. This is the photoperiod switch: the trigger is day length, set by your latitude and the season, not the calendar. The clump bulbs up on whatever leaf count it reached, which is why the leaf stage mattered.

beginner: You cannot make this happen faster, so just keep watering steadily as the clump starts to fill out. If nothing swells, or it swells when the plants are still tiny, you may have the wrong type for your area, which is the thing to fix next year.
seasoned: There is no action that moves this trigger; the work was done in the leaf stage. Keep moisture steady so the swell starts without a check, and confirm you planted a type suited to your latitude.

beginner: Write down when the clumps started to split and how many bulbs each makes. Over time this shows whether your shallot type suits where you live.
seasoned: Note the date division visibly began and how many bulbs each clump sets; over seasons this confirms whether your variety fits your site.

beginner: Write down when you harvested, how long you dried the shallots, and how well they kept. That tells you next year how long to dry them.
seasoned: Record the lift date, curing length, and how the bulbs stored; curing time versus storage life is the feedback that pays off all season.

beginner: When the days reach the right length, the plant stops making leaves and each shoot swells into its own bulb. You cannot speed this up, so just keep watering steadily as the clump fills out. seasoned: Clump division is triggered by day length crossing the cultivar threshold, not by anything you do, so there is no action that moves it; the leaf count reached before the switch sets how many bulbs form and how large. beginner: A shallot is a small, mild onion relative that grows in a cluster. Here is the fun part: you plant one little bulb (called a set) and it splits underground into a bunch of 6 to 12 bulbs, so you dig up a whole clump from each one you planted. Shallots taste sweeter and gentler than regular onions, with a hint of garlic, and they keep for many months once dried. They are the same species as the onion, so like onions they start making bulbs based on how long the days are, not on the calendar. The traditional kinds grown from sets are easygoing about this, but it still helps to pick a type suited to where you live. Give them rich, loose soil and full sun, water them steadily, and they are one of the easiest alliums to grow.
seasoned: Shallot (Allium cepa, Aggregatum group) is a cool-season allium grown for the small, fine-grained bulbs prized for their mild, sweet, faintly garlicky flavor. Its signature is multiplication: plant one set and it divides underground into a cluster of 6 to 12 bulbs, so you lift a whole clump where an onion gives a single bulb. Like the bulb onion it shares a species with, shallot is photoperiodic, a cluster sizes up only once day length crosses a cultivar threshold, which is why the right type tracks your latitude. Traditional set-grown shallots are more forgiving about day length than seed onions, but matching the type to your region still pays off. Grow it like an onion otherwise: a heavy-feeding, shallow-rooted plant in loose, fertile soil, kept evenly moist while the clump fills, then eased off water as the tops fall to begin curing. Well-cured shallots store for months, often longer than onions.

Dig up the whole clump on a dry day, then dry (cure) the bulbs before storing. If you want fresh green shallots sooner, you can pull a few young plants at around 50 to 60 days and use them like green onions.
